The **Empire State Building** is a 102-story,[[c]](#cite_note-Floor_count-10) [supertall](/wiki/Supertall "Supertall") skyscraper in the [Midtown South](/wiki/Midtown_South "Midtown South") neighborhood of [Manhattan](/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), New York City, United States. The building was designed in the [Art Deco](/wiki/Art_Deco "Art Deco") style by [Shreve, Lamb & Harmon](/wiki/Shreve,_Lamb_%26_Harmon "Shreve, Lamb & Harmon") and constructed between 1930 and 1931. Its name is derived from "[Empire State](/wiki/Empire_State "Empire State")", the [nickname](/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_nicknames "List of U.S. state nicknames") of New York state. The building has a roof height of 1,250 feet (380 m) and stands a total of 1,454 feet (443.2 m) tall including its [antenna](/wiki/Antenna_(radio) "Antenna (radio)"). The Empire State Building was the world's tallest building until the [North Tower](/wiki/1_World_Trade_Center_(1970%E2%80%932001) "1 World Trade Center (1970–2001)") of the [World Trade Center](/wiki/World_Trade_Center_(1973%E2%80%932001) "World Trade Center (1973–2001)") was [topped out in 1970](/wiki/Construction_of_the_World_Trade_Center "Construction of the World Trade Center"); following the [September 11 attacks](/wiki/Collapse_of_the_World_Trade_Center "Collapse of the World Trade Center") in 2001, the Empire State Building was once more New York City's tallest building until it was surpassed in 2012 by [One World Trade Center](/wiki/One_World_Trade_Center "One World Trade Center"). As of 2025, the building is the [eighth-tallest building in New York City](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_New_York_City "List of tallest buildings in New York City"), the [tenth-tallest completed skyscraper in the United States](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_the_United_States "List of tallest buildings in the United States"), and the [59th-tallest completed skyscraper in the world](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings "List

fanoutqa_036837.t: Football in London :: History :: part 01 :: chunk_0002
fanoutqa_036837.x:
Football in London :: History :: part 01 :: chunk_0002
The playing of team ball games (almost certainly including football) was first recorded in London by William FitzStephen around 1174–1183. He described the activities of London youths during the annual festival of [Shrove Tuesday](/wiki/Shrove_Tuesday "Shrove Tuesday").

:   "After lunch all of the city's youth would go out into the fields to take part in a ball game. The students of each school have their own ball; the workers from each city craft are also carrying their balls. Older citizens, fathers, and the wealthy would come on horseback to watch their juniors competing, and to relive their own youth vicariously: you can see their inner passions aroused as they watch the action and get caught up in the fun being had by the carefree adolescents."[[3]](#cite_note-4)

Regular references to the game occurred throughout the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, including the first reference to the word "football" in English when it was outlawed by King [Henry IV of England](/wiki/Henry_IV_of_England "Henry IV of England") in 1409. Early games were probably disorganised and violent. In the sixteenth century, the headmaster of [St Paul's School](/wiki/St_Paul%27s_School_(London) "St Paul's School (London)") [Richard Mulcaster](/wiki/Richard_Mulcaster "Richard Mulcaster") is credited with taking [mob football](/wiki/Mob_football "Mob football") and transforming it into organised and refereed team football. In 1581 he wrote about his game of football, which included smaller teams, referees, set positions and even a coach.

Straddling the [Yamuna](/wiki/Yamuna "Yamuna") river, but spread chiefly to the west, or beyond its [right bank](/wiki/Bank_(geography) "Bank (geography)"), Delhi shares borders with the state of [Uttar Pradesh](/wiki/Uttar_Pradesh "Uttar Pradesh") in the east and with the state of [Haryana](/wiki/Haryana "Haryana") in the remaining directions. Delhi became a [union territory](/wiki/Union_territory "Union territory") on 1 November 1956 and the NCT in 1995.[[24]](#cite_note-statesmans-yb-2023-delhi-area-pop-26) The NCT covers an area of 1,484 square kilometres (573 sq mi).[[4]](#cite_note-Delhi_Info-4) According to the 2011 census, Delhi's city proper population was over 11 million,[[7]](#cite_note-2011_census_Delhi-8)[[25]](#cite_note-27) while the NCT's population was about 16.8 million.[[8]](#cite_note-delhi2011-9)

The topography of the medieval fort [Purana Qila](/wiki/Purana_Qila "Purana Qila") on the banks of the river Yamuna matches the literary description of the citadel [Indraprastha](/wiki/Indraprastha "Indraprastha") in the Sanskrit epic *[Mahabharata](/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata")*; however, excavations in the area have revealed no signs of an ancient built environment.[[26]](#cite_note-sunil-kumar2-28)

Under the [Köppen climate classification](/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"), Allentown falls within the [hot-summer humid continental climate](/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") (*Dfa*) if the 0 °C (32 °F) isotherm is used or the [humid subtropical climate](/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") (*Cfa*) if the −3 °C (27 °F) isotherm is used. Summers are typically warm and muggy. Fall and spring are generally mild. Winter is cool to cold. Precipitation is almost uniformly distributed throughout the year.

The average temperature in January is 30.1 °F (−1.1 °C) and the lowest officially recorded temperature was −15 °F (−26 °C) on [January 21, 1994](/wiki/1994_North_American_cold_wave "1994 North American cold wave").[[56]](#cite_note-nws-56) July averages 75.6 °F (24.2 °C) and the highest temperature on record was 105 °F (41 °C) on July 3, 1966.[[56]](#cite_note-nws-56)[[57]](#cite_note-57) January temperatures average below freezing. Seven months average above 50 °F (10.0 °C), and two months average above 71.6 °F (22.0 °C).

Snowfall is variable with some winters bringing light snow and others bringing multiple and significant snowstorms. Average snowfall is 33.1 inches (84 cm) seasonally[[58]](#cite_note-58) with February receiving the highest snowfall at just under 11 inches (280 mm). In 1942, his father was elected to the first of four terms in the [United States Congress](/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress"), and after moving with his family to Washington, D.C., Warren finished elementary school, attended Alice Deal Junior High School and graduated from what was then [Woodrow Wilson High School](/wiki/Jackson-Reed_High_School "Jackson-Reed High School") in 1947, where his senior yearbook picture reads: "likes math; a future stockbroker".[[13]](#cite_note-13) After finishing high school and finding success with his side entrepreneurial and investment ventures, Buffett wanted to skip college to go directly into business but was overruled by his father.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)

Buffett showcased an interest in business and investing at a young age. He was inspired by a book he borrowed from the Omaha public library at age seven, *[One Thousand Ways to Make $1000](/wiki/One_Thousand_Ways_to_Make_$1000 "One Thousand Ways to Make $1000")*.[[16]](#cite_note-16) Much of Buffett's early childhood years were enlivened with entrepreneurial ventures. In 1966, the major leagues moved to the "Deep South" when the Milwaukee Braves moved to Atlanta. In 1968, the Kansas City Athletics moved west to become the [Oakland Athletics](/wiki/Oakland_Athletics "Oakland Athletics"). In 1969, the American and National Leagues both [added two expansion franchises](/wiki/1969_Major_League_Baseball_expansion "1969 Major League Baseball expansion"). The American League added the [Seattle Pilots](/wiki/Seattle_Pilots "Seattle Pilots") (who became the [Milwaukee Brewers](/wiki/Milwaukee_Brewers "Milwaukee Brewers") after one disastrous season in Seattle) and the [Kansas City Royals](/wiki/Kansas_City_Royals "Kansas City Royals"). The NL added the first Canadian franchise, the [Montreal Expos](/wiki/Montreal_Expos "Montreal Expos"), as well as the [San Diego Padres](/wiki/San_Diego_Padres "San Diego Padres").

In 1972, the second Washington Senators moved to the [Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex](/wiki/Dallas%E2%80%93Fort_Worth_metroplex "Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex") to become the [Texas Rangers](/wiki/Texas_Rangers_(baseball) "Texas Rangers (baseball)"). In 1977, baseball [expanded again](/wiki/1977_Major_League_Baseball_expansion "1977 Major League Baseball expansion"), adding a second Canadian team, the [Toronto Blue Jays](/wiki/Toronto_Blue_Jays "Toronto Blue Jays"), as well as the [Seattle Mariners](/wiki/Seattle_Mariners "Seattle Mariners"). Subsequently, no new teams were added until 1993, and no teams moved until 2005.

The average annual temperature ranges from 51 °F (11 °C) on the Pacific coast to 40 °F (4 °C) in the northeast. The highest recorded temperature in the state was 120 °F (49 °C) at [Hanford](/wiki/Hanford,_Washington "Hanford, Washington") on June 29, 2021.[[91]](#cite_note-92)[[92]](#cite_note-93) Both records were set east of the Cascades. Western Washington is known for its mild climate, considerable fog, frequent cloud cover, long-lasting drizzles in the winter and warm, temperate summers. The eastern region, which does not benefit from the general moderating effect of the Pacific Ocean, occasionally experiences extreme climate. Arctic cold fronts in the winter and heat waves in the summer are not uncommon. In the Western region, temperatures have reached as high as 118 °F (48 °C) in [Maple Valley](/wiki/Maple_Valley,_Washington "Maple Valley, Washington")[[93]](#cite_note-94) during the [June 2021 heat wave](/wiki/2021_Western_North_America_heat_wave "2021 Western North America heat wave"), and as low as −6 °F (−21 °C) in [Longview](/wiki/Longview,_Washington "Longview, Washington"),[[94]](#cite_note-95) and even −8 °F (−22 °C) in [Sammamish](/wiki/Sammamish "Sammamish").[[95]](#cite_note-96)

A late-summer wave of COVID-19 cases, as reflected by tests at pharmacies and healthcare settings, marked the first US surge of infections since the end of the public health emergency. Wastewater testing initially indicated that the uptick in cases was only a third the size of the previous summer's surge, yet data from Walgreens showed the first week of August having the largest number of positive cases since May 2021.[[198]](#cite_note-203)[[199]](#cite_note-204)

Hospitals across the United States reported a 24% rise in hospitalizations during the first two weeks of August and wastewater testing showed increased cases in the West and Northeast. With the pandemic legally declared over earlier in 2023, schools and workplaces responded to outbreaks differently, with many schools seeking to be more judicious about when to keep students home from school. The film studio Lionsgate, however, briefly reinstated a mask mandate following an outbreak, as did [Morris Brown College](/wiki/Morris_Brown_College "Morris Brown College"), which also reinstated temperature checks and a restriction on large events for two weeks, at the beginning of the fall 2023 semester.[[200]](#cite_note-205) As more schools launched their fall semesters in late August and early September, high positivity rates among students and staff led to temporary in-person learning suspensions across three school districts in Texas and Tennessee, driven by district-level decisions rather than state authorities.[[201]](#cite_note-206)

It is the [second-most populous city proper](/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Florida "List of municipalities in Florida") in Florida, with a population of 442,241 at the [2020 census](/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census").[[5]](#cite_note-2020CensusPopulationByRace-6) The [Miami metropolitan area](/wiki/Miami_metropolitan_area "Miami metropolitan area") in [South Florida](/wiki/South_Florida "South Florida") has an estimated 6.39 million residents, ranking as the fifth-largest metropolitan area in the [Southeast](/wiki/Southeastern_United_States "Southeastern United States") and [eighth-largest metropolitan area](/wiki/Metropolitan_statistical_area#United_States "Metropolitan statistical area") in the United States.[[7]](#cite_note-2020Pop-8) Miami has the [third-largest skyline](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_the_United_States#Cities_with_the_most_skyscrapers "List of tallest buildings in the United States") in the U.S. with over [300 high-rises](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_Miami "List of tallest buildings in Miami"),[[11]](#cite_note-13) 70 of which exceed 491 ft (150 m).[[12]](#cite_note-14) It is the [county seat](/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Miami-Dade County](/wiki/Miami-Dade_County,_Florida "Miami-Dade County, Florida").

Shapiro](/wiki/Harold_Tafler_Shapiro "Harold Tafler Shapiro") would succeed Bowen and remain president until 2001. Shapiro would continue to increase the endowment, expand academic programs, raise student diversity, and oversee the most renovations in Princeton's history.[[127]](#cite_note-129) One of Shapiro's initiatives was the formation of the multidisciplinary Princeton Environmental Institute in 1994, renamed the [High Meadows Environmental Institute](/wiki/High_Meadows_Environmental_Institute "High Meadows Environmental Institute") in 2020.[[128]](#cite_note-Wohlforth-130)[[129]](#cite_note-Valenti-131) In 2001, Princeton shifted the financial aid policy to a system that replaced all loans with grants.[[130]](#cite_note-Moroz-2001-132) That same year, Princeton elected its first female president, [Shirley M. Tilghman](/wiki/Shirley_M._Tilghman "Shirley M. Tilghman").[[131]](#cite_note-Horwitz-2001-133) Before retiring in 2012, Tilghman expanded financial aid offerings and conducted several major construction projects like the Lewis Center for the Arts and a sixth residential college.[[132]](#cite_note-134) Tilghman also led initiatives for more global programs, the creation of an office of sustainability, and investments into the sciences.[[133]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurkee202214-135)

*Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows* was released in hardcover on 21 July 2007[[48]](#cite_note-49) and in paperback in the United Kingdom on 10 July 2008[[49]](#cite_note-50) and the United States on 7 July 2009.[[50]](#cite_note-51) In [SoHo, New York](/wiki/SoHo "SoHo"), there was a release party for the American paperback edition, with many games and activities.[[51]](#cite_note-52) An "Adult Edition" with a different cover illustration was released by Bloomsbury on 21 July 2007.[[52]](#cite_note-53) To be released simultaneously with the original US hardcover on 21 July with only 100,000 copies was a Scholastic deluxe edition, highlighting a new cover illustration by Mary GrandPré.[[53]](#cite_note-54) In October 2010, Bloomsbury released a "Celebratory" paperback edition, which featured a foiled and starred cover.[[54]](#cite_note-55) Lastly, on 1 November 2010, a "Signature" edition of the novel was released in paperback by Bloomsbury.[[55]](#cite_note-56)
